steps.title: Keep the nearest surface
steps.goal: Draw two overlapping triangles in depth, keeping the nearer one visible even when it is drawn first.
steps.trace: Vertex z → transformed depth → depth comparison → colour written only for the nearer fragment
steps.question: Why is it not enough to draw the far triangle first?
steps.answer: A particular draw order might work for these two flat triangles, but a real scene can overlap differently from each viewpoint. A depth attachment remembers the nearest depth at each pixel. The comparison chooses visibility there, so drawing an opaque farther surface later does not cover a nearer one.
steps.story:
Keep the nearer triangle even when the farther triangle is drawn last. Give pink depth 0.25 and turquoise depth 0.75; draw pink first.

Attach a depth texture alongside colour. Clear depth to 1 and use `Less` with depth writes: a fragment passes only when it is nearer than the stored depth. Its dimensions and sample count must match the colour image.

A vertex now contains position and colour: six `f32` values, 24 bytes. Shader locations 0 and 1 read those two groups. The vertex shader passes colour to the fragment shader.

The browser supplies the startup dimensions to `renderer.resize`. Later resize handling updates both attachments. This depth rule handles opaque visibility; transparency comes later.

![Two fragments compete at one pixel; the depth test keeps 0.25 and rejects the later fragment at 0.75.](../illustrations/journey-10.svg)
steps.result: Look at the overlapping triangles. The nearer triangle must cover the farther one even though it is drawn first. Reverse their draw order: the overlap should stay the same. Restore the order.
steps.experiment: Temporarily change the near triangle’s three z values from 0.25 to 0.9. Predict which colour will appear at the shared centre. Turquoise should now win. Restore the values, then reverse the two groups of indices: the picture should stay the same. Restore the original order before comparing.
steps.production: The finished viewer uses depth attachments for opaque visibility, then adds the rules needed for strokes, CAD boundaries and transparency. This lesson establishes why those rules must refer to visible surfaces rather than draw order.
steps.browser_status: The nearer pink triangle wins the overlap.

steps.title: Give geometry a validated CPU owner
steps.goal: Own validated mesh values and a scene collection before uploading them.
steps.trace: Mesh::new validates owned vectors → Scene retains Mesh values
steps.question: Why return slices rather than mutable vectors?
steps.answer: A borrowed slice lets upload read the values without transferring ownership or allowing invalid indices to be inserted.
steps.story:
Mesh owns vertex and index vectors. Its constructor rejects missing vertices, incomplete triangles and nonfinite values. Scene owns a collection of those validated meshes.

Vec owns its allocation; a slice borrows existing elements. Result returns either the constructed Mesh or the reason it was refused. GPU upload consumes these slices in the next step.

![Validated vectors become Mesh values retained by Scene.](../illustrations/journey-direct-10a-mesh.svg)
steps.result: Inspect the supplied state fixtures. Valid triangles are accepted; missing vertices, incomplete triangles and NaN values are rejected.
steps.experiment: In the constructor test, replace the invalid index 3 with 2. That case becomes valid, so its is_err assertion should fail. Restore 3.
steps.production: The viewer validates source geometry before deriving GPU data. This checkpoint establishes CPU ownership and constructor checks; the next checkpoint connects that data to drawing.
steps.browser_status: The nearer pink triangle wins the overlap.
steps.browser_caption: The browser retains the preceding depth image and command dock. Native constructor and scene-collection checks establish the new CPU behavior; browser upload is connected next.

steps.title: Draw the scene through GPU mesh owners
steps.goal: Add and remove a mesh through scene data while reusing the renderer and camera.
steps.trace: Example Triangle → Scene changes → set_scene uploads → GpuMesh draws
steps.question: Does uploading transfer the CPU Mesh to the renderer?
steps.answer: No. upload borrows &Mesh; Scene keeps the original vectors while GpuMesh owns the copied GPU buffers.
steps.story:
GpuMesh owns the vertex and index buffers uploaded from a borrowed Mesh. Renderer owns the uploaded list; the browser retains Scene.

Example Triangle changes the CPU collection, uploads it, then redraws. Camera commands update only the view uniform.

The upload borrows validated slices and copies their bytes into buffers. Replacing those buffers leaves the CPU scene and camera owned by the caller.

![CPU Scene and Mesh values supply derived GpuMesh buffers to Renderer.](../illustrations/journey-direct-11-scene.svg)
steps.result: Type Example Triangle. A third, green triangle appears.
steps.experiment: Pan Right, then submit Example Triangle twice. The scene should return to the same image without resetting the camera.
steps.production: The production viewer keeps source geometry and document state separate from packed GPU data. Later lessons add stable identity, incremental synchronization, shared buffers and undo. This ownership boundary allows a GPU rebuild without rebuilding the document.
steps.browser_status: Scene data owns the meshes; the renderer displays them.

steps.title: Name objects independently of their rows
steps.goal: Keep object identity stable when removal changes vector order.
steps.trace: Scene allocates ObjectId → Object retains Mesh → GPU upload borrows that mesh
steps.question: Does moving to row zero create a new object?
steps.answer: No. The vector position changes; the ObjectId assigned at insertion stays the same.
steps.story:
ObjectId names an object independently of its vector row. Scene allocates IDs, looks up objects by those names, and remembers the extra triangle by ID.

The wrapper type prevents confusing an ID with an index. checked_add returns an error before the counter can wrap and reuse a name.

![An object keeps its ID when removal shifts its vector row.](../illustrations/journey-direct-11a-identity.svg)
steps.result: Inspect the supplied state fixtures. Removing the first object moves the next row without changing its ID; toggling the extra object still removes that object.
steps.experiment: In the removal test, compare the second object’s ID before and after deleting the first. The ID should match even though its row changes.
steps.production: Source identities and GPU row positions have different lifetimes. This checkpoint keeps the source name stable while the existing upload borrows each object’s mesh.
steps.browser_status: Scene data owns the meshes; the renderer displays them.
steps.browser_caption: The browser independently verifies the retained add/remove drawing and command dock. Native tests establish stable IDs and removal after row changes; selection display is connected next.
